summary:
Vitalis is a health-monitoring system that lets astronauts on long-duration missions assess and act on their own health when real-time ground support isn’t available. Crew members log daily indicators, and Vitalis compares them against each person’s personal baseline, using drift detection and rolling z-score anomaly analysis to catch gradual changes linked to radiation exposure, isolation, altered gravity, immune shifts, bone loss, cardiovascular strain and behavioral health decline.

A deterministic rules engine alone decides health status, so critical decisions are transparent and never left to an AI’s guess. A Groq-hosted LLM then explains the status in plain language and guides next steps, using retrieval over an onboard medical knowledge base so its answers stay grounded. Optional NASA DONKI space-weather data adds environmental context.

This matters because communication delays make Earth-based care impractical on deep-space missions. Vitalis combines the reliability of rule-based logic with the accessibility of AI, supporting crew autonomy and earlier intervention. It is a decision-support prototype built on synthetic data, not a medical device.
details:
What it does and how it works
Vitalis helps astronauts on long missions monitor their own health when Earth can’t respond quickly. Crew members log daily health indicators. A rules engine compares them with each person’s own baseline and uses drift detection to set a health status. A rolling z-score anomaly detector adds advisory flags. The system then retrieves relevant guidance from an onboard medical knowledge base, and a large language model (LLM) explains the status and next steps in plain language. Optional NASA DONKI space-weather data adds radiation context.

Benefits

  • Catches slow health changes early, because it compares each person to their own baseline rather than a population average.
  • Gives clear, readable guidance without waiting on ground support.
  • Keeps the status transparent and testable, because rules set it and the AI never does.

Intended impact
The goal is to support crew autonomy and earlier intervention on deep-space missions, where communication delays make real-time medical help impractical. It is a decision-support prototype built on synthetic data, not a medical device.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React progressive web app (PWA) built with Vite and TypeScript.
  • Backend: Node.js with Fastify.
  • Database: Supabase Postgres with row-level security.
  • AI: Groq-hosted LLM, with retrieval using TF-IDF over markdown knowledge files.
  • Data: NASA DONKI API, cached.
  • DevOps and testing: Docker Compose, GitHub Actions, and in-process PGlite with a mocked LLM so tests need no accounts.
  • Hardware: none. It runs on standard computers and uses synthetic data.

How it is creative

  • It separates deterministic logic from AI: rules decide, the LLM only explains.
  • It uses personal baselines instead of generic thresholds.
  • It combines a rules engine, anomaly detection, retrieval and space-weather data in one lightweight tool.
  • It is built to be reproducible, with fully offline tests.

Factors the team considered

  • Safety and trust: AI should not make critical health decisions, and the prototype is clearly labeled as non-medical.
  • Privacy and security: the database is backend-only with row-level security.
  • Reliability: reproducible tests and the risk of the free-tier database pausing.
  • Realism: the real constraints of spaceflight, such as delayed contact and the need for crew independence.
  • Data: synthetic data, since real astronaut data is private.
dataRefs: NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information)
